1:
The figure of arming is taken up by all who touch it. Robertson notes that the verb comes from the word for a weapon and is metaphorical here, found nowhere else in the New Testament. Ellicott would render the noun conception rather than mind, and denies that it means merely putting oneself into the same disposition, that is, resolving to die with Christ: Christ was armed with a particular view of the suffering itself, a sufficient shield in the day of it, and we are exhorted to try the same defensive armour. Wesley calls it armour of proof against all our enemies, and Calvin says we are supplied with invincible weapons if we partake as we ought of the efficacy of Christ’s death. Henry finds the point in a shift of sense: flesh means Christ’s human nature in the first half and man’s corrupt nature in the second, so that as Christ suffered in the one we are to make the other suffer.

Whether the words for us belong to the text is raised only by Ellicott, who reports that two editors strike them out and thinks them right, and holds that neither they nor the variant for you is wanted, the point here being not the atoning character of the death but the death itself. Gill builds on the phrase the opposite way, that Christ suffered not for himself nor for angels but for men, and not for all men, since his death with respect to some must then be in vain, but for the elect.

What having ceased from sin means draws four answers, and Clarke sets them out. Taken as a general maxim, the man who suffers reflects on his ways, is humbled and fears approaching death, the mind losing its relish for the sins of the flesh. Some take it of those who have resolved to suffer death rather than apostatize, and have therefore ceased from the sin of saving their lives at the expense of their faith. Others make it parallel to the sixth of Romans, that he who has mortified the flesh has ceased from sin. The fourth he reports and refuses, that the whole is of our redemption and means that Christ suffering in the flesh died for our sins, a very constrained sense. Calvin rejects the same reading independently, ascribing it to Erasmus and answering that the sentence is indefinite and extends to all the godly, as in the words of Romans about him who is dead being freed from sin. Robertson puts it plainly: temptation has lost its power with such a man.

Ellicott meets the difficulty the verse creates for Christ himself. If death is rest from sin, Christ too in dying ceased from sin; and he answers from the grammar, that the verb means to have been caused to rest, the apostle using the part of it which denotes not a voluntary stopping but a pause imposed from without, so that Christ found in death a boon of rest from sin, though the words do not say from sinning. On the following verse he presses a second point of grammar: the Greek admits equally the plural, that ye no longer should live, which attaches the clause to the arming rather than to the sufferer; otherwise the apostle slides from urging martyrs to face bodily death into the baptismal death to sin, and is left making a martyr’s death a step towards living the rest of one’s life becomingly. Robertson renders the plural; Gill reports the Arabic doing the same. Calvin finds in the verse the two parts of renovation, the destruction of the flesh and the vivification of the spirit, the first to begin with and the second to advance to. Clarke reads the lusts of men as the will of the idolatrous persecutors; Barnes takes the whole as the object of redemption, to rescue us from wicked lusts.
3:
Two words of the English are disputed. Gill reports that our is left out in the Alexandrian copy and in the Latin and Syriac versions, and prefers the Arabic reading, the time of your past life, since the apostle would hardly put himself among those who had walked in the sins about to be named. Ellicott strikes out two, of our life and us, the first a scribe’s addition and the second a filler after the word suffice, and says that if they stood the apostle would be identifying himself with a life he never led. Barnes defends the received text: the apostle says we not because he had been addicted to these vices but as speaking of Christians in general, since it is common to say that we lived so and so of a body of people without meaning that each was guilty of all.

What may suffice means is guarded by Calvin, who denies that the apostle would have us wearied with pleasures as men filled to satiety are, and holds instead that the memory of our past life is the sharpest goad to repentance. Ellicott hears irony in the word and would render it, sufficient is the past; Barnes matches it with a line of Horace on having had one's fill; Robertson notes that the adjective occurs elsewhere only in Matthew and may echo a saying of Christ. On the will of the Gentiles the two part company. Barnes says it means not subservience to their will but doing what they did. Ellicott makes the word a wish and not a will, and takes the clause to mean the doing of the bad things the heathen wanted them to be guilty of, since the heathen were fain to catch them at malpractices.

Clarke sets the catalogue out as a complete epitome of the heathen state, six items with their Greek: every species of impurity, strong irregular appetites, being inflamed with wine in continual debauches, lascivious feastings with drunken songs, drinking matches, and the abominations practised at idol feasts. Ellicott adds the philology: the first word should be plural, for repeated acts, and means any outrageous debauchery, so that it may include all that follow; excess of wine is a contemptuous term, wine-swillings, while banquetings is more refined and implies company. On the drink Barnes enters a caution: nothing can be determined from this word about the moderate use of wine, the apostle having his eye on such use as led to intoxication. Robertson presses the other way, finding it strange that modern Christians justify a personal liberty to drink and carouse. Wesley asks whether the last two words have any meaning now, and answers that they had seventeen hundred years ago, when meetings to eat and to drink were ranked with abominable idolatries.

Who the readers were is the question the last item raises. Clarke takes the catalogue as proof that those addressed had been Gentiles, and Ellicott reports the same argument as the main support of those who hold the letter written to converts from heathenism, asking how the apostle could tell men brought up as Jews that the past was long enough for abominable idolatries; these, he notes, are called abominable not as idolatries but for the adjuncts of the idol feasts. Gill and Calvin keep the Jewish readership and account for the sins by mixture, Calvin saying the apostle reproves the Jews for mingling with the Gentiles in their pollutions though the Lord had separated them. Calvin then raises the objection that the apostle seems to wrong many, since some Gentiles lived honourably, and answers that he charges no individual with all of them, but that we are so far under the power of depravity that such fruits proceed from it as from an evil root: no one lacks the seed of all vices, though all do not germinate in every man.
4:
The word for thinking it strange is glossed alike. Robertson takes it from the word for a stranger and renders it, they are astonished, the phrase for running with them meaning to run together like a crowd; he quotes the judgment that Christians had to stand aloof from the world’s social pleasures and were resented as enemies of all joy and so of the human race. Calvin says the word means to stop at a thing as new and unusual, as when Cicero calls himself a stranger in the city because he knew not what was carried on there; and he reports the taunt in its own words, that these must form for themselves a new world, since they differ from all mankind.

Why the change seems strange is answered at length by two. Barnes gives three reasons: they cannot appreciate the motives of those who leave them, living for themselves and never directing the mind to the account they must render; they do not see the guilt and folly of sinful pleasures; and they do not feel the force of the argument for religion. He adds that the kindred of the Saviour thought him beside himself and Festus thought Paul mad, and that fool, enthusiast and fanatic occur to the heart even when not allowed to escape the lips. Henry lists what puzzles them: that these should despise what everyone else is fond of, believe what to others seems incredible, delight in what is irksome, and depend so much upon hope. Ellicott takes the opening word grammatically, holding that it points not back to the list of sins but forward to the participle, so that the sense is, in a particular where they cannot imagine your not being as bad as themselves, slanderously affirming that you are; the participle stands in the wrong case, but he notes the apostle handles participles freely.

On the evil speaking Clarke says the word is literally blaspheming, uttered impiously against God and calumniously of the readers, and Wesley supplies the epithets: proud, silly, wicked. That the slanderers must answer is urged as a comfort. Gill says the apostle writes it to calm God’s people, that they may sit easy under censures and not avenge themselves; Calvin makes the coming judgment the support against all assaults, since Christ will punish those who now condemn us and show that our cause is approved by him; Ellicott hears an echo of the earlier chapter, where these same persons call the Christians to give account, and finds a side purpose, to warn the readers against sharing their fate by sharing their sins.

How ready the Judge is divides them. Barnes denies that the words mean the day was near at hand, whatever the apostle may have supposed, and takes them to mean only that he was prepared, all the arrangements being made and nothing hindering. Ellicott goes the other way, placing the clause a step further along the history of Christ, after the sitting at the right hand, in the order of the Creed, and quoting Bengel that the Apostles, when not expressly treating of the date of the advent, set it before their longing as close at hand, so that Peter reckons the slanderers of his own day among the living about to be judged. Robertson prefers the reading, to the one readily judging, saying the smoother rendering softens the rugged original; he takes the judge for Christ here, though the Father earlier. Who the quick and the dead are is a further question. Barnes and Robertson take them as those alive at the coming and those already dead; Calvin adds that the dead are named lest we think we lose anything if our slanderers outlive us. Clarke alone reads the pair of two nations, the Gentiles dead in trespasses and sins before the Gospel came, and the Jews having by profession a name to live.
6:
Ellicott begins by disowning the English. The version is misleading, he says, and seems one of those rare cases where the original has been expanded by the translators for doctrinal ends, the Greek being simply, to the dead also, or more literally, to dead men also; and no one with an unpreoccupied mind could doubt, taking the clause by itself, that those preached to were dead at the time. Gill enters a smaller correction, that the opening words look forward and not back, and that what follows states not the reason of the preaching but the event consequent on it.

One family of readings takes the dead as the spiritually dead. Barnes reports Doddridge and Whitby so understanding it of the Gentiles, brought to such a state of life as their carnal neighbours would count a kind of condemnation and death; Clarke gives two renderings on the same footing, one punishing the unconverted Gentiles as carnal men while others lead a spiritual life, the other holding that the gospel was preached to the Gentiles that, though condemned by men in the flesh, they might live eternally by God in the Spirit. Robertson traces the spiritual sense to Augustine and Luther, reports the objection that the apostle could not use one word in two senses so close together, and answers that Christ did exactly that with the word for life within a single sentence.

The other family takes the dead literally, and divides again over which dead. Barnes prefers those then dead who had heard the gospel while living and become Christians, on three grounds: it is the natural meaning of the word, the apostle had just used it so in the previous verse, and it suits a letter to the persecuted, for whom it was an encouragement that those already put to death still lived to God. Ellicott takes the verse back to the earlier chapter and makes it a further explanation of the purpose of Christ’s descent. Clarke prefers the antediluvians, the apostle referring to the same fact as before, so that the gospel was preached by Noah to a world then condemned, which hearing might believe and live to God in the Spirit. Barnes reports two more, the sinners of the old world, with a hope that some were saved, and those who had suffered martyrdom. Calvin holds that Christ was made known as a redeemer to the dead, and draws the consequence: if the grace of Christ once penetrated to the dead, we shall partake of it when dead, and we set for it limits much too narrow if we confine it to the present life. He adds that the words anticipate the objection that the gospel is of no benefit to the dead, since it does not restore them to life. Robertson reports a further view, that all who did not hear the message in this life will hear it in the next before the judgment.

The two clauses that follow are read as a single contrast. Barnes sets them side by side: so far as men were concerned they were condemned and put to death for their religion, and so far as God was concerned they were given life. Calvin says judged here means, as often elsewhere, condemned, and that though by the world’s estimation the dead suffer destruction in the flesh, they do not cease to live with God in their spirit, because Christ quickens them by his Spirit, which will at length absorb the relics of death that still cleave to us. Robertson marks the same opposition between the phrase according to men and the phrase according to God. Wesley makes the judgment rash and unrighteous and the life a soul renewed after God’s image. Clarke, keeping his own reading, makes it a case of mercy, men already condemned by righteous judgment being granted a respite in which they might hear and believe.
7:
What end is meant divides them. Clarke takes it of the destruction of Jerusalem by the Romans, then a very few years off, so that the end intended is that of the temple, the Levitical priesthood and the whole Jewish economy; and he finds the apostle keeping the deluge in view, since God had said to Noah in the same words that the end of all flesh was come before him. Henry takes the same destruction first but adds that their own lives and their enemies’ will soon reach their period and that the world itself will not continue long. Gill allows three senses at once, the end of each man's life, of the Jewish church and state, and of the whole frame of this world. Calvin refuses the national reading outright, saying there is no ground for it and that it is strange such a notion should be entertained, and takes the words of the universal renovation of the world.

How near it stands is pressed less confidently. Barnes grants that the phrase would naturally mean the winding up of human affairs, but is not certain the apostle used it so, since death is to each man the end of all things here below; he traces the verb through its uses of nearness in place and in time and concludes that it means close by. Robertson says how near the apostle does not say, but urges readiness as Christ and Paul did, adding that it draws nearer all the time yet is not at once. Ellicott is franker: probably, he says, if the apostle had thought the world would stand twenty centuries more he would have expressed himself differently. Calvin faces the same objection and answers it: the time seems long to us because we measure its length by the spaces of this fleeting life, but if we could understand the perpetuity of the life to come, many ages would appear a moment. From the time Christ appeared, he adds, nothing is left for the faithful but to look forward with suspended minds to his second coming; were the trumpet to sound in our ears it would rouse us and not suffer us to lie torpid.

The two imperatives are distinguished by the grammarians. Ellicott says the first includes more than sobriety and means keeping a check on all the desires, while the usual notion of sobriety is given more exactly by the second; and he corrects the English again, that unto prayer is a slip for unto prayers, so that we are not merely to be always in a frame to pray but to have actual prayers on our lips, every incident of life suggesting them. He adds that the tense of the imperatives implies that the readers had slipped into a careless state and needed rousing. Robertson renders the first, be ye of sound mind, the noun being plural.

Whether the sobriety is of body or mind is disputed. Calvin assigns both words to the mind rather than the body, since as surfeiting and sleep unfit the body for its duties, so the vain cares and pleasures of the world inebriate the mind and make it drowsy. Henry takes the body seriously in its own right, holding that its right ordering promotes the good of the soul, since when its appetites are restrained by God’s word and its interests submitted to the soul’s, the body is not the soul’s enemy but its friend and helper; and he adds that those who would pray to purpose must watch over their own spirits and take all fit opportunities. Clarke makes it a prudent and moderate use of all one possesses, with watching against every occasion of sin and prayer for a supporting hand. Wesley states the connection as a circle: temperance helps watchfulness and both help prayer, so watch that ye may pray and pray that ye may watch.
8:
The force of the exhortation is felt in the adjective. Ellicott says the original is far more vigorous, before all things keeping intense your charity toward yourselves, the apostle assuming the charity is there and insisting only that it not be suffered to flag. Robertson renders it the same way and traces the word to a verb meaning to stretch out; Barnes says it means properly extended, and so earnest and fervent; Clarke gives it as intense love. Calvin makes it the first thing, the bond of perfection, and finds the reason for the strong word in a contrast: whoever is fervent in self-love loves others coldly. Gill widens the circle, that love is due to all men and even to enemies but especially to the saints, not only those of the same nation or church but all the saints everywhere; and he grounds the priority plainly, that outward sobriety and watchings and prayer are nothing without it.

Where the saying comes from is disputed. Barnes and Calvin take it as a quotation from Solomon, and Calvin expounds the original by its two contrasted clauses: since hatred is there the cause why men traduce one another, the contrary effect is ascribed to love, that men who love one another courteously forgive, burying each other’s vices and seeking to preserve another’s honour. Ellicott doubts it, since the words differ widely from the Greek version of that place and vary from the Hebrew too, and since the same variation appears in the Epistle of James; he thinks it likelier that the proverb was current and familiar to both writers, and warns that it is therefore unsafe to argue from the shade of meaning the words bear in Proverbs. He also corrects the tense: the right reading is neither shall nor will but covereth.

Whose sins are covered is settled alike by all who raise it. Robertson puts it in a phrase, the sins of the one loved and not of the one loving. Barnes says true love makes us kind to another’s imperfections and often blind to their existence, and quotes the couplet that love is gentle, delicate and kind, to faults compassionate or blind. Clarke says a loving disposition leads us to pass by the faults of others and excuse their transgressions as far as truth allows. Wesley carries it into prayer, that he who loves turns his own eyes from another’s faults and hides them as far as he can, and continually prays that the sinner’s iniquities may be forgiven, while the God of love measures to him with the same measure. Ellicott reports the Hebrew sense, that to cover often means to forgive, the image being of an offensive object buried under something else, so that where an enemy rakes up every old grudge, one who loves will not let even himself see the wrongs done him by a friend; but he finds that reading strained here and prefers the sense the words bear in James.

One inference is refused by three of them independently. Barnes says the words do not mean, as the Romanists maintain, that charity procures us pardon, since besides being contrary to the uniform teaching of Scripture that departs from the obvious meaning of the passage; Clarke says flatly that our love to others will not induce God to pardon our offences; Calvin says it appears from this how absurd are those who elicit their own satisfactions from the place. Barnes also distinguishes the saying in James, which he takes of sins covered so far as God is concerned, from this one, of sins covered so far as we are concerned. Calvin ends on the number: Solomon says not that a few sins are covered but a multitude, as Christ bids us forgive seventy times seven; and where loose reins are given to hatred, men must consume one another by mutual biting and tearing.
9:
Hospitality is treated as the first form the charity takes. Ellicott regrets that the participial clauses are broken up in our version into separate injunctions, since the Greek runs on, being hospitable; and he makes this the receiving of Christians from other towns, adding that such hospitality is seen covering a multitude of sins, to the surprise of the bestowers, in the parable of the sheep and the goats. Gill renders the word as being lovers of strangers, who are not to be vexed or oppressed but counselled and, if need be, given food and lodging; the light of nature has led men to it, he adds, instancing Jethro toward Moses and the islanders of Melita toward Paul. Robertson supplies the circumstance that made it necessary: inns were rare and very poor, and hospitality made mission work possible. Calvin says it was then commonly used and deemed a sacred kind of humanity, and notes that the apostle bids it be mutual, so that no one require more from others than he is himself prepared to render.

The added words are read as forbidding not reluctance but complaint. Barnes says the Greek is without murmurs, and that grudging in the common sense, of doing a thing unwillingly or regretting the expense, is not exactly the idea: it greatly enhances the value of hospitality that it be done with entire cheerfulness, one of the duties being to make a guest happy by showing him that he is welcome. Ellicott turns it into a rebuke, how frequently Christian hospitality is marred by grumbling at the expense and the trouble it costs. Robertson says simply that complaint spoils hospitality, and Clarke that nothing is to be done merely because commanded but from love to God and man, and then it will be without grumbling. Calvin remarks that it is a rare example for a man to spend himself and his own upon his neighbour without any disparaging reflection.

What the gift is divides them. Robertson takes it as one of the gifts of the Holy Spirit. Clarke says he cannot think the word means the Holy Ghost here, or his supernatural gifts, though it may include them, and that it signifies anything given by the mere bounty of God, though in this place he suspects it means some office in the Church, which the connection seems to require. Barnes takes it as endowment of any kind, especially that conferred by the Spirit, and here as every endowment by which we can do good to others. Ellicott notes that there is no article in the Greek, so that it might be rendered, according as every man was gifted, and says it is hard to tell when these gifts were received. Wesley allows spiritual or temporal, ordinary or extraordinary, but thinks the extraordinary primarily intended. Gill sorts them into three, special grace, the ministerial gift, and the gifts of nature and providence.

The steward is what the rest turns on. Ellicott says no one receives these gifts as his own but is only a steward, so that when he offers them to the Church it is not as a benefactor but as a servant, ministering; and he takes grace here not in its theological sense but in the sense of bountiful giving, praising the word rendered manifold for the variety it gives to God's bounty, though the emphatic word is of God. Robertson glosses the same word as many-coloured. Barnes says we are appointed by God to do this work for him, and Clarke that whatever gifts a man has are the Lord’s property. Calvin makes the diversity deliberate: nothing corrects our murmurings better than to remember that we do not give our own, and the Lord has so divided his graces that every one needs his brother’s help, a bond heathens have noticed but which God appointed on purpose, to bind men one to another.
11:
What the oracles of God are is the first dispute. Gill takes them for the writings of the Old Testament, so called because they come from God and are infallible, and holds that a preacher’s matter must be fetched out of them. Ellicott refuses that: the article is not in the Greek, so the phrase cannot be pressed to mean the model of the Old Testament, and the emphatic word is of God, the preacher being not to trust his own powers or seek applause but to act as one possessed of powers not his own. Robertson lands between them, noting that the phrase is used elsewhere of the Mosaic law, of the Old Testament and of Christian teaching, and taking it here of God’s utterances through Christian teachers. Clarke allows both the immediate influence and the revelation already given, and adds that the command reaches every man in holy orders, in pretended holy orders, or pretending to holy orders.

Calvin will not let the particle soften the charge. It is not introduced, he says, as though it were enough to profess that what is taught is God’s word, which was commonly the case with the false prophets of old; the apostle forbids any man to go forth except one instructed in God’s word who proclaims infallible oracles as it were from his mouth. He adds that if teachers considered that in teaching the oracles of God they are the representatives of Christ, there would be much more fidelity in them, whereas carelessness comes of the majesty of the word being borne in mind by so few. Wesley turns the verse into a test of true and false prophets: the oracles of God teach that men should repent, believe and obey, and he who treats of faith and leaves out repentance, or does not enjoin practical holiness on believers, does not preach Christ, however highly he thinks of himself.

The second clause is taken of money, not office. Barnes allows that the word might mean the office of a deacon but thinks it does not, since that office had charge of the church’s funds, whereas the words about the ability God giveth imply the distributing of what was a man’s own. Ellicott is flat that it means not spiritual service of any kind but the giving of this life’s good things to the poor, since the word rendered ability often expresses, like our word resources, a sufficiency of wealth; and he traces the verb rendered giveth to paying the expenses of putting a play on the stage, a public burden borne at Athens by the wealthier citizens in turn. Robertson takes the same word to its root in the chorus leader but concludes rather that God is the supplier of strength. Clarke agrees that the ministering is the care of the poor, and presses the consequence that the actor is not the author, so that whoever gives as from himself robs God. Barnes states the rule in a line: none is bound to go beyond his ability, and every one is required to come up to it.

Ellicott alone reads the paragraph as one argument for liberality. The clause about speaking, he holds, is not complete in itself but introduced to give point to what follows, since it is easy to recognise in spiritual things the principle of God being all in all, and the apostle bids them apply it to material gifts: as the preacher is a mere mouthpiece of God, so the giver is but God’s dispenser, that in this too God may have all the glory. On the doxology Robertson notes that the relative most naturally refers to Jesus Christ as the immediate antecedent, though elsewhere such doxologies are offered to God through Christ. Wesley divides the terms, the glory of the wisdom that teaches us to speak and the might that enables us to act.
12:
Whether the trial is present or coming turns on grammar. Ellicott calls the English rendering not only slovenly but false in the impression it gives, since the fiery trial was not future but actually present: literally, be not bewildered at the conflagration among you taking place for a trial to you. Robertson agrees, taking the participle as already coming, and traces the word to the smelting of gold and silver in the Old Testament. Barnes reads it the other way, of a persecution then impending, and grants that we cannot determine precisely what it was, nor press the word to prove they were to suffer literally by fire. Clarke calls the metaphor old but noble, faith tried as gold is tried; Wesley thinks it includes martyrdom by fire as well as the sufferings before it.

Why they should not be bewildered is variously answered. Ellicott notes that the verb means literally to feel like people in a strange country, lost and bewildered, and that these Christians felt at first that a life of sorrow was not to be expected by followers of the Messiah. Calvin says they ought by long meditation to have been prepared beforehand to bear the cross, since whoever has resolved to fight under Christ’s banner will bear persecution as one accustomed to it. Henry adds that an unmortified spirit is unfit to bear trials, and that there is no reason to wonder at the world’s unkindness since Christians are forewarned of it and Christ endured it. Clarke numbers five arguments: that persecution is no strange thing for God’s people; that suffering as Christ did ends in glory with him; that the Spirit supports them meanwhile; that it is an honour to suffer as a Christian and not as a malefactor; and that the weight of the storm falls at last on the unbelievers.

Whose sufferings they share is narrowly defined. Gill says they are not partakers of Christ’s personal sufferings, though they enjoy the benefits of those, but of the sufferings of his body the church, which is mystically himself, called his because of the union between him and his people. Barnes says they are sufferings of the same kind he endured and for the same reasons. Calvin draws two uses from the cross, that God thus tries our faith and that we become partakers with Christ, and holds the second by far the greater; the wicked also bear afflictions, but being separated from Christ they apprehend nothing but wrath, so that sorrow and dread overwhelm them. Ellicott presses the measure, taking the conjunction to mean in proportion as, and illustrates it from the acts of Probus, a Cappadocian martyr who, when nails were heated and driven through his hands, cried out, Glory to Thee, Lord Jesus Christ, who hast deigned to let my hands be pierced for Thy name’s sake.

The joy is twofold. Calvin distinguishes the joy we now have in hope from the full fruition Christ’s coming will bring, the first mingled with grief and the second joined with exultation, and guards the point: it is not suitable in affliction to think of a joy that frees us from all trouble, but the consolations of God moderate our evils so that we can rejoice at the same time. Ellicott attaches the purpose to both earlier commands, so that we are neither bewildered nor merely enduring but rejoicing, in order that at the revelation of his glory we may rejoice exulting; such rejoicing now, he says, is a sure means to rejoicing in glory hereafter. Barnes marks the two stages differently, that a good man has joy when at death he is received into his Saviour’s presence, but complete joy only when before assembled worlds he hears the sentence confirming him in happiness for ever. Wesley states the proportion plainly: the measure of glory answers the measure of suffering, and much more abundantly.
14:
Why reproach is singled out Calvin explains: there is often more bitterness in it than in the loss of goods or in bodily torment, since many strong to bear want and bold to meet death yet succumb under reproach. Ellicott says the Spirit is called the Spirit of glory as he is elsewhere called the Spirit of truth, glory standing in contrast with reproach; and lest it be doubted who is meant, the apostle adds, and of God, which is the climax, since God is greater than his own glory. The verb resteth, he says, means far more than remaineth, expressing the complete repose with which the Spirit abides on men who have the hearts of martyrs. Robertson gives the image in a line, that the Spirit rests on the Christian as the Shechinah rested on the tabernacle. Barnes finds the practical point, that persecutions occasion a more copious effusion of the Spirit, so that it is often gain to suffer. Clarke reports a various reading, and of power, found in many manuscripts and versions; Calvin notices a different division of the words but prefers the received one.

Why the caution against crimes is needed Ellicott explains from history. The Greek, he says, takes the opposite turn, for let none of you suffer, so that the apostle calls them happy because he is sure they will not pretend to die as martyrs when they are really dying as criminals; and he recalls how largely the first converts were drawn from criminal classes, citing a bishop of Carthage who had to expose men that courted persecution to cloak their crimes. He adds that Pliny, governing these same men a little later, found that they bound themselves by oath not to any crime but to commit no theft or adultery, to break no promise and to repudiate no liability.

The fourth term is the puzzle. Barnes says it occurs nowhere else in the New Testament, means properly an inspector of the things of others, and is best taken of one who busies himself with what does not concern him. Clarke adds a political reading, that some think meddling with those in public office is meant, the readers being to leave public officers to their own master. Ellicott calls it a droll word and reports that the zealous who declaimed against the pagans were humorously called bishops of those without, while this word means bishops of other men’s matters. Robertson thinks the apostle coined it and observes that its second element is the word for bishop, so that it may hint at preachers meddling in the work of other preachers. Calvin dissents from all of them and makes it covetousness, one who gapes after plunder and inquires into the affairs of others with crooked eyes.

The name itself carries the sting. Ellicott says the apostle purposely uses what was then a name of derision, not one believers would ordinarily take to themselves; well-bred people avoided pronouncing it, and Tacitus speaks of those vulgarly so known. He holds it an open question whether we should not read the barbarous form Chrestian, since the oldest manuscripts have it and a scribe who called himself a Christian would hardly turn the familiar word into a strange one. Robertson reports the same spelling and the same contempt, and remarks that the apostle had once been ashamed of a sneer for being a disciple but is not ashamed now. Gill says the name was first given at Antioch and, being agreeable, was retained. Calvin regards not the name but the cause, since whatever words the adversaries used it was enough that the faithful suffered for the Gospel. Ellicott would render the last clause, let him glorify God in this name, making even the name of ridicule the ground of an act of glory; and Wesley says God gives both the honour so to suffer and the reward.
17:
What the house of God is divides them. Gill allows either the temple at Jerusalem, now about to be left desolate, or the church of God. Barnes reports that many take it of the Jews and the doom of the holy city, but holds the obvious reference to be Christians, and finds an allusion to the vision where the destroyer is told to begin at the sanctuary. Ellicott takes it the same way and draws the two halves of the chapter together: those who bear the mark of the Christ’s shame on their foreheads and are not ashamed of it are safe in this judgment, since the command was to come not near any man upon whom is the mark. Clarke supplies a rabbinic parallel almost in the apostle’s own words, that God never punishes the world but because of the wicked, yet always begins with the righteous, the destroyer making no difference between just and unjust except that he begins there.

What the judgment is, and whether a text is quoted, are further questions. Barnes takes the word for the severe trial that determines character. Gill denies that it is punishment for sin strictly speaking, since Christ endured that in their room, and makes it fatherly chastisement. Ellicott would read the judgment, the great one all expect, and notes that the word begin shows a long process, so that the apostle probably does not distinguish the present burning from the final judgment except as its beginning. Calvin denies that any particular passage is referred to, holding that the apostle took the sentence from the common teaching of Scripture, since the Lord always exhibited the first examples of his chastisements in his own people, as the head of a family corrects his own children rather than strangers.

How the righteous are scarcely saved is the sharpest question. Barnes says the word implies difficulty, so that the thing came very near not to happen, and grants that there are perils which jeopard their salvation, though they would be saved, in a manner showing that to human appearance it was doubtful. Gill guards the point exactly there: not as if they were but in part saved, for the salvation is complete, nor as if it were doubtful, for though scarcely, yet certainly they are saved. Ellicott reports the older opinion, that scarcely imports no uncertainty in the thing itself but only difficulty in the way, and answers that this is only partly true, since the apostle thinks of the final judgment and means that little margin was left, a very few more falls and they would have been lost; when the best of us looks back in the light of the last day, he adds, he will be amazed that he could be saved at all. Clarke reads it historically: the Christians escaped from Jerusalem with extreme difficulty but every man of them escaped, withdrawing to Pella, while not one of the Jews escaped.

That the words come from Proverbs is agreed, and the fact troubles one of them. Ellicott calls it a literal quotation of the Greek version and evidence of the apostle’s familiarity with both texts, since he elsewhere rejects that version where it does not suit him and here accepts it though it differs from the Hebrew. Clarke calls the same fact rather strange and says such a latitude of construction can scarcely be accounted for, setting the Hebrew, the Chaldee, the Syriac, the Arabic and the Latin side by side. Calvin draws the argument from the less to the greater: if God spares not his own children whom he loves, dreadful will be his severity against the rebellious. Robertson enters one caution, that the Christian is not saved by his own righteousness; Wesley notes that the salvation primarily spoken of is temporal, though the words may be applied to eternal things, and are then still more awful.
19:
What suffering according to the will of God means is disputed. Clarke takes it morally: a man suffers so who suffers for righteousness’ sake and, being reviled, reviles not again; Wesley says the same in six words, both for a good cause and in a right spirit. Ellicott refuses that reading: the clause means not suffering in a godly and unblameable manner, as against suffering as a murderer, but that such a death is no accident but stands in strict accordance with God’s prearranged design; and he notes that our version omits a little word, so that it should run, let even them that suffer, the stress lying on being put to death. Barnes and Gill go the same way, Barnes taking it of the sufferings Providence shall appoint and Gill insisting that these are not the effects of chance nor of men’s malice but are by God’s appointment, for their good and his glory. Calvin adds the comfort in it, that we suffer nothing except by the permission of God.

The verb of committing is a banker’s word. Ellicott calls it a technical term for depositing a deed or a sum of money with someone in trust, and traces it elsewhere to doctrine left in trust; but the words the apostle probably had ringing in his ears, he says, are those of our Lord on the cross, where the same verb is used, Father, into thy hands I commend my spirit. Robertson notices the same two things independently, calling it a banking figure and the word Jesus used as he died. Wesley calls the soul a sacred depositum, and Calvin paraphrases the whole as a delivering of themselves and their life to the safe keeping of God.

Whether the word means souls or lives follows from that. Ellicott says it might perhaps with still more propriety be rendered their lives, and draws the connection out: mild as these trials are beside the terrors overhanging the sinful, even if the worst comes and a man must die a martyr’s death, it is but the execution of God’s plan for him; let him view his life as a deposit and lay it confidently in God’s hands, to be returned when the time comes. Barnes takes the word as equivalent to themselves, so that they were to leave everything in God’s hand, faithfully performing every duty and not being anxious for the result; Wesley adds the qualification, whatever becomes of the body.

The last title is where Calvin parts from the rest. The Greek word, he says, means both creator and keeper, and he prefers the second, since by bidding us deposit our life with God the apostle makes him its safe keeper; and he is called faithful because he faithfully keeps and defends whatever is under his protection. Ellicott agrees that faithful is used with reference to the deposit placed in his hands, but keeps Creator, and remarks that the title seems chosen here in preference to Father. Barnes builds on the same title: as Creator, God will be faithful to the design he had in view, since he abandons no purpose he has formed, and did not create us that we might be miserable, nor does he wish it. Clarke attaches a condition: God is faithful because he will always fulfil his word and withhold no good thing from them that walk uprightly, but they had no reason to hope he would care for their lives unless they continued in well-doing, since the path of duty ever was and ever will be the only way of safety. Barnes states the balance more mildly, that a man engaged always in well-doing may safely commit all his interest to God; and Robertson notes that the word for well-doing occurs nowhere else in the New Testament.
